precedingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: Let R1 name the red-associated allele, or version of the flower-colour gene, and R2 the white-associated version. The small 1 and 2 are labels attached to R. Each complete symbol names one allele; the number does not count chromosomes or tell us to multiply. In plain text, the same symbols are written R1 and R2. A diploid plant has two copies at this locus, so R1R1 and R2R2 each describe a homozygote, while R1R2 describes a heterozygote with different versions.

precedingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: In the image, begin with the two flowers at the top. Match the red flower to R1R1 and the white flower to R2R2. The cross sign connects the chosen parents. Follow their arrows to the pink flower below, then compare its two allele symbols with the symbols in the parents. The complete picture is visible; read those levels in order to keep parentage clear.

followingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: The starting parents are the P generation. Their offspring are the F1 generation. A normal gamete contributes one allele at this locus: the red parent contributes R1 with probability 1, and the white parent contributes R2 with probability 1. Fertilisation joins an egg and a sperm, restoring the allele pair. Every available pairing in this cross is therefore R1R2, with probability 1 × 1 = 1. The single pink flower stands for that offspring category, not a counted sample of one plant.

followingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: Now compare the expressed colours. The phenotype, the characteristic we observe or measure, is pink in the heterozygote, between the red and white homozygote appearances. That relationship is incomplete dominance. We name it from the comparison of genotypes and their phenotypes, rather than from the colour pink by itself.
followingExplanatoryParagraphs.quoteConvention: Exact parsed text content; native sub/sup elements are represented by their contained characters, not an invented plain-text allele spelling.

followingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: In this flower model, the red-associated allele contributes to red-pigment production. A heterozygote has one red-associated copy out of its two allele copies and makes less red pigment than the red homozygote, giving an intermediate pink appearance. It still has two copies of the locus, R1 and R2. The colour does not mean that the DNA versions have fused into a new pink allele. Nor does incomplete dominance require every intermediate phenotype to arise through exactly the same pigment mechanism.

followingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: At position A, top IA meets side IB, giving IAIB. Both antigen types are expressed, so the phenotype is AB. At position B, top i meets side IB, giving IBi and phenotype B. At position C, top IA meets side i, giving IAi and phenotype A. At position D, the two i contributions meet, giving ii and phenotype O.

followingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: Each of these four cells gives a different genotype and a different phenotype. Consequently, this cross predicts ¼ AB, ¼ B, ¼ A and ¼ O. The genotype ratio is 1 IAIB : 1 IBi : 1 IAi : 1 ii. The phenotype ratio, in the diagram's position order, is 1 AB : 1 B : 1 A : 1 O. Four equal quarters total 1, so the complete set is accounted for.

followingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: The two contributions explain why an allele can be inherited without being apparent in a parent's ABO category. Each heterozygous parent carries i, even though neither is type O. An ii offspring can receive one i from each. Conversely, an AB offspring needs IA from one parent and IB from the other. Read the needed contributions rather than assigning offspring a blend of the parents' blood-group names.

We are not inferring both parents to be heterozygous just from their A and B appearances.

precedingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: The chromosome mechanism has not changed. DNA is copied before meiosis. Homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis I, and sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, with no additional DNA copying between those divisions. In flowering plants, meiosis first produces haploid spores; later stages maintaining the haploid set produce the structures that form gametes. The result needed here is one allele at this locus in an egg or sperm. Copying and separation retain the R1 and R2 versions.

precedingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: Under equal segregation, each pink parent contributes R1 with probability ½ or R2 with probability ½. Incomplete dominance changes the plant's expressed colour, not those gamete probabilities. We also assume random fertilisation: the allele in the egg does not favour one of the possible sperm alleles. That is why we can multiply the two contribution probabilities for a particular offspring pair.

precedingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: Read the table with sperm contributions across the top and egg contributions down the left. Each outside label is a single allele in a gamete. Each interior entry joins the allele above it to the allele beside it, forming an offspring genotype. Both row weights and both column weights total 1.

followingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: At the upper left, R1 meets R1, giving the red homozygote. At the upper right and lower left, different parental routes bring one R1 and one R2 together. Reversing their order does not create another genotype in this ordinary autosomal model. At the lower right, each parent contributes R2, producing a white homozygote. White is possible because the parents carried and transmitted that version even while their own flowers were pink.

followingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: The four distinct contribution routes have total probability ¼ + ¼ + ¼ + ¼ = 1. For genotype grouping, add the two routes to the heterozygote: ¼ + ¼ = ½. The genotype ratio is 1 R1R1 : 2 R1R2 : 1 R2R2. All three genotypes have distinguishable colours here, so the phenotypic ratio, the relative proportions of appearance categories, is also 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. The ratio belongs to these parents and this expression rule.
followingExplanatoryParagraphs.quoteConvention: Exact parsed text content; native sub/sup elements are represented by their contained characters, not an invented plain-text allele spelling.

followingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: Suppose 96 offspring plants from this cross are grown and scored. An expected count is the model's average predicted count for groups of that size. Multiply each phenotype probability by 96: red gives 96 × ¼ = 24, pink gives 96 × ½ = 48, and white gives 96 × ¼ = 24. The counts total 24 + 48 + 24 = 96, and the underlying probabilities total 1. We have assumed reliable expression and no selective loss of a genotype before scoring.

Retain the flower-colour rules R1R1 red, R1R2 pink and R2R2 white. The two loci assort independently, fertilisation is random, and these phenotypes are expressed reliably. precedingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: Two genes can also affect the same visible characteristic. Making a pigment and placing that pigment in a petal are different jobs. If the second job does not occur, the petal's appearance may not reveal which pigment the first gene would otherwise produce. We need that kind of expression rule to interpret the optional coat-colour problem that follows.

precedingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: Consider an explicitly hypothetical plant model with two independently assorting loci. P/p controls pigment identity: P_ specifies purple pigment, while pp specifies amber pigment. P_ means PP or Pp; the underscore stands for the second allele at the P locus. D/d controls whether the pigment is deposited in the petal. D_, meaning DD or Dd, allows deposition. With dd, neither pigment is deposited and the petal is pale. These are the stated rules for this model, not a claim about every real flower.
precedingExplanatoryParagraphs.quoteConvention: Exact parsed text content; native sub/sup elements are represented by their contained characters, not an invented plain-text allele spelling.

precedingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: Read the deposition pair first in the table. If it is dd, the visible colour is already settled. If it is D_, inspect the P/p pair to decide which pigment appears. This order makes the dependency in the biological explanation visible.

followingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: This is gene interaction: the phenotype associated with one locus depends on another locus. In this example, dd masks the visible effect of the P/p pair, a form of interaction called epistasis. The P alleles are still present and can be transmitted. Their colour effect is not visible under dd. This differs from incomplete dominance or codominance, which compare allele expression within one locus. It also differs from adding many small contributions to a continuously varying trait.

We are given the genotypes, so we do not have to infer the second D-locus allele from appearance. Assume ordinary equal segregation, independent assortment, random fertilisation and reliable expression, with no genotype category selectively lost before scoring.
followingExplanatoryParagraphs.quoteConvention: Exact parsed text content; native sub/sup elements are represented by their contained characters, not an invented plain-text allele spelling.

The ppDd parent contributes p with certainty and D or d at ½ each. It therefore has two distinct gametes, pD and pd, each with probability 1 × ½ = ½. The first list totals four quarters and the second totals two halves, so each accounts for all of that parent's contributions.

precedingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: The partner's AB phenotype identifies IAIB. Both antigen-associated alleles are needed, and there is no i in that pair. We can now write the justified cross as IBi × IAIB. This step must come before the square: beginning with a guessed homozygous B parent would change the prediction.

precedingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: The woman contributes IB or i in eggs at ½ each. The partner contributes IA or IB in sperm at ½ each. Put the egg contributions down the left and sperm contributions across the top. Each interior pairing has probability ½ × ½ = ¼ under random fertilisation.

followingExplanatoryParagraphs.textContent: The upper-left cell joins IB from the egg with IA from the sperm, producing AB. The upper-right joins two IB copies, producing B. The lower-left joins i with IA, producing A. The lower-right joins i with IB, also producing B. The four genotypes are distinct and equally probable, so their genotype ratio is 1:1:1:1 in that cell order.

Type A has probability ¼ and type AB has probability ¼. Type O requires ii and is impossible under these parents because the AB partner cannot supply i.
